papers.title: JAX-Nano: A GPU-Accelerated Differentiable Phonon Boltzmann Transport Solver for Nanoscale Heat Transfer
papers.abstract: As semiconductor device dimensions approach phonon mean free paths, heat transport enters ballistic and quasi-ballistic regimes where Fourier's law becomes inadequate. The phonon Boltzmann transport equation (BTE) describes these nonequilibrium effects but presents significant computational challenges. This work introduces JAX-Nano, a GPU-accelerated, end-to-end differentiable phonon BTE solver for nanoscale heat transport. The solver integrates steady-state and transient BTE formulations within a unified finite-volume framework, supporting structured and unstructured meshes, mode-resolved transport, phonon scattering, volumetric heat generation, and multiple boundary conditions. Automatic differentiation enables gradient computation with respect to transport properties, boundary conditions, heat-generation rates, and geometric parameters without separately derived adjoint equations. Numerical predictions are validated against analytical solutions and established BTE solvers across diffusive-to-ballistic regimes. Applications to complex three-dimensional geometries are demonstrated using single-fin, double-fin, and arrayed fin field-effect transistor (FinFET) configurations. Gradient-based inverse learning enables single- and multi-parameter identification, including simultaneous recovery of mode-resolved phonon relaxation times and spatially distributed heat-generation rates in steady-state and transient problems. GPU performance and scalability are evaluated with respect to spatial resolution, angular discretization, and phonon bands, including comparisons with an MPI-based BTE solver. JAX-Nano provides a unified computational framework for three-dimensional phonon transport, automatic differentiation, and inverse parameter identification, enabling sensitivity analysis and optimization of nanoscale thermal systems.

papers.title: Beyond PINNs: Boundary-Enriched Holomorphic Networks for Laplace Problems
papers.abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) solve partial differential equations by penalizing their residual, but this formulation can be difficult to optimize for solutions with singular behaviour. We focus specifically on the two-dimensional Laplace equation, whose strong analytical structure allows the governing equation to be enforced directly in the neural representation. We compare a hybrid harmonic-neural model with a holomorphic neural network whose output is harmonic by construction and therefore requires only boundary training. We further enrich the holomorphic model with singular functions chosen according to the interior angle and boundary conditions at each junction of boundary segments. On six singular benchmarks, the enriched model is the most accurate of the neural models we compare. On the four with a closed-form solution, however, that solution lies in the span of the enrichment terms, and a least-squares fit of these terms alone is exact to rounding error. On Motz's problem and the cracked beam, the neural core reduces the relative error of the recovered leading singular coefficient from about $10^{-2}$, for a least-squares fit with the same four terms, to about $10^{-6}$, and on four variants whose solution has a smooth part outside the span, the network is $4\times10^{4}$ to $2\times10^{7}$ times more accurate than a fit of its singular terms alone; classical least-squares fits with more singular terms, or with harmonic polynomials and rational poles, are more accurate still. Our results demonstrate how exploiting problem-specific analytical structure can provide an alternative to base and residual PINNs for challenging scientific computing problems.

papers.title: A new frequency-time hybrid RPML-BIE solver with few-mode corrections for the wave-equation problems in nonuniform closed waveguides
papers.abstract: This paper is devoted to proposing a novel FTH integral equation solver for wave-equation problems in two-dimensional nonuniform closed waveguides with multiple channels. The FTH methodology, which combines the Fourier transform with frequency-domain BIE formulations, has demonstrated its effectiveness in solving time-dependent wave scattering problems. However, when applied to waveguide problems, the modal expansions arising from multiple scattering introduce cut-off frequencies. Such frequencies pose significant challenges, requiring both a frequency-robust solver for frequency-domain waveguide problems and an efficient treatment of the solution's non-smooth behavior near the cut-off frequencies for the evaluation of the inverse Fourier transform. The first issue is addressed by developing a new frequency-domain BIE method based on the free-space fundamental solution and regionalized perfectly matched layer truncation, together with a few-mode Dirichlet-to-Robin modification. The method is rigorously proved to achieve uniform exponential convergence, even at frequencies arbitrarily close to the cut-off frequencies. To address the second issue---the recovery of the time-domain solution via the inverse Fourier transform---a sine-transform based stationary-point Filon--Clenshaw--Curtis quadrature is introduced to accurately handle the non-smoothness and square-root singularities of frequency-domain solutions. Additionally, theoretical result shows that the complex resonances closing to the real axis may significantly effect the convergence of the Fourier transform algorithm and then a novel strategy of complex resonance extraction based on AAA rational approximation and singularity subtraction is utilized to avoid this influence. Numerical experiments for both frequency-domain and time-domain problems illustrate the efficiency and high accuracy of the proposed method.

papers.title: A particle method for the space homogeneous Lenard-Balescu equation
papers.abstract: We propose a structure preserving particle method to numerically approximate the spatially homogeneous Lenard-Balescu equation for collisional plasmas. The Lenard-Balescu operator is an improvement of the Landau equation with a dielectric function taking the dynamic screening effect into account. Our particle method is based on the variational formulation of the Lenard-Balescu equation under suitable regularization analogous to the strategy followed for the Landau collision operator in [12]. The method guarantees the conservation laws and the entropy dissipation at the semi-discrete level. The novel difficulty of the nonlocal nonlinear dependence of the dielectric function is tackled by rewriting it as integrals in terms of orthogonal and parallel components to the frequency variable. This equivalent form reduces the evaluation of the dielectric function to numerically computing an integral of the directional derivative of the solution on a hyperplane orthogonal to the frequency variable and its one-dimensional Hilbert transform. An efficient implementation of the numerical approximation for the Lenard-Balescu kernel is derived by exploiting this expression of the dielectric function. We finally validate our method by means of several numerical tests, further allowing us to explore qualitative properties of the Lenard-Balescu equation.

papers.title: Expressive Shallow Networks for Physics-Informed Learning: Why Curvature-Aware Optimization and FP64 Are Not Enough
papers.abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) often struggle with high-frequency and high-order partial differential equations (PDEs) due to optimization stiffness and spectral bias, despite possessing sufficient approximation capacity. Existing remedies, including modified feature representations, domain decomposition, higher floating-point precision, and curvature-aware optimizers, can improve convergence but largely act as workarounds for optimization difficulties arising from deep architectures rather than addressing their underlying source. We investigate Physics-Informed Shallow Universal Polynomial Networks (PI-SUPNs), which replace deep nonlinear compositions with learnable polynomial expansions, retaining high approximation capacity within a shallow computational graph. On a high-frequency Helmholtz benchmark, PI-SUPNs are the only architecture to successfully recover the solution, while all competing models fail even under FP64 precision and curvature-aware optimization. However, experiments on higher vibrational modes of a fourth-order Euler-Bernoulli beam reveal that architectural improvements alone are insufficient: accurate solutions require the combination of PI-SUPNs, FP64 precision, and curvature-aware optimization. Additionally, Allen-Cahn experiments show that PI-SUPNs achieve lower solution and derivative errors at reduced computational cost, with more favorable loss landscapes than competing architectures. We also establish quasi-local approximation properties and spline-based convergence bounds for SUPNs. Our results show that shallow network architectures are an important mechanism for improving physics-informed trainability, but accurate solutions to the most challenging PDEs can still require FP64 precision and curvature-aware optimization.

papers.title: Accelerating wave-scattering simulations with learned search directions
papers.abstract: Wave-scattering simulation requires solving a dense boundary-element system for every frequency, incidence and design. Krylov solvers build each search space from scratch, and it grows with problem size. Here we present BEMFormer, a solver that learns to generate search directions across systems of one integral equation and supplies geometry-specific directions through a coarse-grid correction. BEMFormer generalizes to unseen geometries, meshes and excitations, and to acoustic scattering after fine-tuning on eight geometries. It reproduces the measured radar cross-sections of benchmark targets. On a quadcopter with 1.04 million unknowns, 38 times the largest training problem, BEMFormer solves each system 30 times faster than a preconditioned Krylov solver. Both reach a radar cross-section deviation of about 1 dB, comparable to the difference between independent measurements and acceptable for engineering applications. These results show that solving million-unknown scattering problems in minutes is possible when the search space is learned rather than built from scratch.

papers.title: An equivariant classical density functional for ionic fluids at complex interfaces
papers.abstract: Predicting the combined effects of ionic packing and long-range electrostatics at complex interfaces is technologically important, but remains challenging without atomistic simulations. Here we present a machine-learned classical density functional for ionic fluids that combines a symmetry-adapted neural free energy for short-range correlations with explicit long-range electrostatics. Trained on three-dimensional equilibrium densities and bulk correlations of the full-Coulomb restricted primitive model, a single functional transfers to charge-patterned particles and atomically structured electrodes. Around anisotropic charged solutes, it reproduces the ionic structure and mean forces from molecular dynamics, including reversals of the bare electrostatic force. At metal electrodes, self-consistent coupling to metal atoms captures the redistribution of ionic and electrode charge and the loading-dependent capacitance enhancement produced by steps and bumps. Combined with mobilities determined independently from bulk molecular dynamics, the same functional describes the main features of charging dynamics and resolves geometry-dependent spatial relaxation. This framework can be extended to more complex ionic fluids, enabling efficient exploration of how composition and geometry control structure and response.

papers.title: Learning free energy across a differentiable temperature range by deep generative modeling
papers.abstract: Free energy governs the directionality, stability, and temperature sensitivity of physical, chemical, and biological transformations. Conventional free energy calculations, such as thermodynamic integration and free energy perturbation, often have to be performed at individual temperatures and are limited by the high cost of sampling an extensive set of thermodynamic states. Here, we introduce learned temperature-differentiable free energy perturbation (TD-FEP), a deep generative framework that learns a temperature-conditioned, invertible mapping between reference and target systems through data-free, energy-based optimization. TD-FEP thereby unifies one-shot state generation and free energy calculation across a continuous temperature range. We validated TD-FEP across a broad range of applications, including isolated molecules, periodic materials, and chemical reactions.

papers.title: A shock-fitting approach to high-order simulation of viscous hypersonic flows based on inviscid implicit shock tracking
papers.abstract: This work presents a framework for computing viscous, shock-dominated flows at high Mach and Reynolds numbers in which the bow shock is located by inviscid implicit shock tracking and then treated as a boundary of the viscous computation. The high-order implicit shock tracking (HOIST) method is applied to the Euler equations on a coarse, shock-agnostic mesh to produce a shock-aligned mesh and the shock geometry; the elements upstream of the shock are discarded, the post-shock domain is remeshed to resolve the boundary layer, and the compressible Navier-Stokes equations are solved on it with a high-order interior penalty discontinuous Galerkin method, with the post-shock state prescribed along the shock boundary by the oblique shock relations. Because the shock structure is never resolved, the approach requires neither the extreme element compression nor the specialized formulations that fully coupled viscous shock tracking demands at these conditions; the tracking optimization is confined to the coarse inviscid mesh, and the viscous computation involves no mesh unknowns and no additional nonlinear stabilization. The framework is demonstrated on a Mach 10.6 axisymmetric blunt cone, a Mach 17.6 cylinder, and a Mach 5 sphere in three dimensions, with surface pressure and heat flux in good agreement with experimental measurements and reference computations.

papers.title: Topological analysis of permeability tensor in anisotropic porous media
papers.abstract: The permeability of an anisotropic porous medium is a tensor whose off-diagonal components, which describe the deflection of the macroscopic flux away from the driving force, are small and change sign under reflections. We ask whether direction-aware topological data analysis can predict the full permeability tensor of three-dimensional porous media directly from their geometry. We introduce two direction-aware topological descriptors for flow problems: a cone-based filtration, adapted from our earlier work on the elastic stiffness tensor, and a throat-scale filtration built on the distance transform of the pore space. Using permeability tensors computed with the lattice Boltzmann method, we compare them with a comprehensive set of non-topological baselines, comprising statistical microstructure descriptors and physics-based permeability estimators. The topological descriptors are most informative for the off-diagonal components, which the baselines capture least well. There the throat-scale filtration alone outperforms every non-topological descriptor set, including the union of all statistical descriptors and physics-based estimators, and adding it to the baselines consistently improves the prediction. We also confirm the approach on real rock data.

papers.title: Cyclic changes of frame for designing non-retracing verification cases for numerical interface tracking
papers.abstract: A forward-backward deformation test supplies an exact final interface, but retracing can allow errors from the two halves to cancel. We construct alternative tests by superposing a cyclic change of frame on the same base deformation. The frame returns to its starting pose, preserving the exact final phase and the deformation history up to rigid placement. A small returning translation can keep trajectories close to the retraced ones. A full rotation about a fixed centre or axis gives closed paths with nonzero winding for material labels that stay off that centre or axis. For incompressible base fields the transformed velocity is divergence-free. We construct discretely solenoidal face fluxes for geometric volume-of-fluid advection by circulating the transformed potential. In three TwoPhaseFlow benchmarks, with a shared time grid for each pair, a full-turn frame increased the final cell-average shape discrepancy in all 30 comparisons, with a median factor of 1.50. The fitted convergence exponent decreased in each of the six benchmark-reconstruction comparisons over the tested grids.

papers.title: Deep Learning of Solver-Aware Turbulence Closures from Nudged LES Dynamics
papers.abstract: The differentiable physics paradigm may be leveraged as an a-posteriori approach for discovering turbulence closure models by embedding a neural network parameterization directly inside the solver and optimizing it given potentially sparse target data. This addresses a key limitation of a-priori learning where direct numerical simulation (DNS) data is used to approximate the subgrid stress with the assumption of a low-pass filter. Closures trained in this a-priori manner frequently lead to unstable deployments due to the mismatch between the assumed filter and the effect of numerical discretizations and coarse-graining. In comparison, while typically stable during deployment, a-posteriori learning incurs high computational costs due to the need to backpropagate through a large eddy simulation (LES) solver. Furthermore, a-posteriori methods are challenging to apply broadly since they require significant modification of existing solvers. Finally, both approaches are limited when generalization is desired across different numerical schemes with their implicit filtering characteristics. In this work, we present a deep-learning approach for turbulence closure modeling built on the continuous data assimilation framework. Our approach enables the a-priori training of closures using DNS data observed only at coarse-grid points without modifying or differentiating through the LES solver, while preserving stability during deployment for the recovery of long-term statistics. We focus on the model's ability to adapt to different discretizations by explicitly conditioning it on the numerical scheme. We use two- and three-dimensional canonical cases to test our framework and show that the learned correction systematically tracks the discretization error of the coarse solver.

papers.title: Equivariant learning of a transferable three-dimensional classical density functional
papers.abstract: Liquids exhibit collective behavior that depends sensitively on thermodynamic conditions, interfaces and confinement, yet predicting each new state commonly requires a separate atomistic simulation. Classical density functional theory offers a reusable variational description, but its central excess free-energy functional is generally unknown, and learned approximations for fluids have largely been developed in reduced-dimensional geometries. Here we show that this functional can be learned directly from fully three-dimensional canonical equilibrium density fields while preserving spatial symmetry and variational consistency, without free-energy or chemical-potential training labels. A functional learned from coarse three-dimensional density fields remains predictive at finer resolution, separating the sampling demands of training from the spatial resolution of subsequent predictions. A single learned functional transfers across temperatures, system sizes and statistical ensembles, and recovers the equation of state, liquid--vapor coexistence and interfacial broadening, none of which are used as training targets. Applied to complex three-dimensional geometries, it predicts the potential of mean force between colloids due to solvent mediation, and adsorption isotherms in an interconnected gyroid pore. These results demonstrate that molecular dynamics equilibrium density data can be converted into a transferable thermodynamic generator connecting microscopic liquid structure to response, phase behavior and collective phenomena.

papers.title: Scaling Density Functional Theory with Gaussian Splatting
papers.abstract: Density functional theory (DFT) strikes a practical balance between accuracy and computational cost in many problems of computational chemistry and materials science. However, many DFT calculations are limited by fixed atom-centered basis sets, which dictate how accuracy and cost scale with system size. We propose Gaussian Splatting for Density Functional Theory (GS-DFT), which represents molecular orbitals as a cloud of Gaussians whose positions, shapes, and mixing coefficients are optimized jointly by gradient descent to minimize the energy without training data. Conceptually, GS-DFT is 3D Gaussian splatting with the renderer replaced by quantum mechanics. We introduce two key solver components: adaptive density fitting with screening for efficient evaluation of two-electron integrals, and a regularized differentiable orthogonalization of the molecular orbitals. Empirically, the optimized basis reaches the accuracy of the largest conventional basis sets with a fraction of the parameters, converging systematically in energy, density, and nuclear forces. At equal parameter count, it captures the stretched-bond and anion physics that fixed bases only recover with specialized basis augmentation. The resulting solver exhibits quadratic peak memory scaling in the cloud size, allowing us to simulate systems of up to 2,742 atoms (10,406 electrons) without any modifications at triple-zeta scale using a single four-GPU node.

papers.title: High-fidelity simulation and reduced-order modeling of optical pumping in quantum devices
papers.abstract: Predicting spin polarization and light attenuation in optically pumped atomic devices requires solving the coupled diffusive quantum master equation (DQME)--light system. Its nonlinearity, spatially nonlocal coupling, and physical admissibility constraints make high-fidelity numerical simulation challenging. We develop a structure-preserving high-fidelity solver that combines second-order finite differences for three-dimensional atomic diffusion, explicit pseudo-time marching for atomic populations, and an exponential integrator for light propagation. Under a derived time-step restriction, the solver preserves population normalization and nonnegativity, as well as the positivity and monotonic attenuation of the light intensity. Three complementary test cases based on an analytical reduction, asymptotic limits, and an analytical invariant are constructed to verify the solver. To accelerate repeated parameter queries, we eliminate the light field and construct a reduced-order model (ROM) using proper orthogonal decomposition and Galerkin projection of the resulting integro-differential formulation involving only atomic populations. An exact quadratic expansion of the spin-exchange term and discrete empirical interpolation of the optical-pumping term make the cost of evaluating the reduced operators independent of the full-order dimension. Numerical tests verify the solver and demonstrate ROM accuracy outside the training set. The GPU implementation completes simulations with millions of unknowns in minutes, while single-core ROM evaluations take seconds, achieving respective speedup factors exceeding 150 and 7000 relative to the single-core high-fidelity solver.

papers.title: Interstitial Magnetoelectricity in Altermagnetic Electrides
papers.abstract: Electrides and altermagnets are two distinct yet intriguing classes of quantum materials, characterized by interstitial anionic electrons and nonrelativistic spin splitting, respectively. The recent prediction of Stoner-instability-driven altermagnetic electride provides a natural bridge between these two fields. Here, we investigate the magnetoelectric response and its related spin-polarized transport in the altermagnetic electride Zr$_2$N monolayer. Using the tight-binding Hubbard model and first-principles calculations, we find that the electric field can break the magnetic compensation between the two interstitial anionic electrons, inducing a finite net magnetization and giving rise to an interstitial electron mediated magnetoelectric response. The magnetoelectric response is further demonstrated through the electrical control of spin conductivity. Our results reveal a magnetoelectric effect in altermagnetic electrides, paving a way towards electride-based spintronic devices.

papers.title: CLFF: Automated Framework for Concurrent Learning Force Fields and Material Property Calculations
papers.abstract: Machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) offer an efficient paradigm for large-scale atomistic simulations with near first-principles accuracy. However, developing and deploying these potentials often involves intricate procedures that require substantial manual effort and domain expertise. In this work, we present CLFF, an open-source Python framework designed to automate concurrent learning workflows for MLIPs. CLFF integrates model training, MLIP-driven sampling, uncertainty-based candidate selection, quantum-mechanical labeling, and dataset augmentation into a unified workflow. The framework currently supports several modern graph-based MLIP architectures and is compatible with widely used computational chemistry and materials science tools. A distinguishing feature of CLFF is its ability to asynchronously distribute computational tasks across multiple heterogeneous remote computing resources, enabling users to aggregate fragmented hardware infrastructure within a single controllable workflow. In addition to concurrent learning, CLFF provides automated workflows for initial data generation and material property calculations, including phonon dispersion and potential energy surface scans. By minimizing manual intervention and enhancing reproducibility, CLFF offers a flexible platform for developing and deploying MLIPs in computational materials research.

papers.title: AmorphGen: A Python package for amorphous structure generation with machine-learning and classical interatomic potentials
papers.abstract: AmorphGen is an open-source Python package for generating and analyzing amorphous structures from a composition or a crystal. Chemically informed rules estimate initial densities and assign separation and coordination constraints. Three routes are available: random placement followed by relaxation, melt-quench from a crystal, and a hybrid route that anneals and quenches random structures. ASE provides access to classical and machine-learning potentials, with GPU batching for selected backends. Analysis tools compute coordination numbers, bond angles, rings, and X-ray or neutron structure factors for comparison with measurements. An optional interface to the FEFF code computes extended X-ray absorption fine structure (EXAFS) spectra. For amorphous Ga2O3, TiO2 and InGaZnO4, the cation coordination numbers are close to reference models and measurements, and the X-ray structure factors reproduce the main measured peaks. The EXAFS spectra for Ga2O3 and InGaZnO4 also capture the dominant first-shell features observed experimentally. The hybrid route reduces bonding defects in SiO2 and As and builds the first sharp diffraction peak of SiO2. By simplifying ensemble generation and standardizing structural assessment, AmorphGen makes it practical to compare amorphous models across compositions, potentials, and preparation routes, and to screen new amorphous compositions.

papers.title: MagPot: A magnetoelastic potential generator for molecular dynamics simulations
papers.abstract: Magnetoelastic phenomena originate from the coupling between atomic displacements and magnetic degrees of freedom, and their atomistic simulation requires interatomic models in which magnetic interactions depend explicitly on interatomic distance. This paper presents MagPot, a Python program that generates Bethe-Slater parameter sets for spin-lattice molecular dynamics simulations using the SPIN package of the Large-scale Atomic/Molecular Massively Parallel Simulator (LAMMPS). From a compact set of material properties, the program determines the radial functions describing Heisenberg exchange and the dipole and quadrupole contributions of the two-ion N\'eel interaction. Version 1.0 supports simple-cubic, body-centred-cubic and face-centred-cubic lattices with ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic configurations. A central feature of MagPot is its modular architecture, which allows the magnetic contribution it generates to be combined additively with a broad range of compatible non-magnetic interatomic potentials. The parameterisation workflow is assessed through equation-of-state, Curie-temperature, volume-magnetostriction, pressure-dependent magnetocrystalline-anisotropy and anisotropic-magnetoelastic tests. By automating the construction of the magnetic contribution to the interatomic model, MagPot offers a straightforward and reproducible route from material properties to LAMMPS-ready magnetic interactions, facilitating large-scale atomistic simulations of magnetoelasticity and magnetostriction, as well as physical phenomena associated with magnon-phonon coupling.

papers.title: A Unified Energy-Density Framework for Moir\'e Interface Energetics and Mechanics
papers.abstract: The mechanical response of moir\'e interfaces depends on how atomic registry combines with contact size and boundary geometry. An analytical description must retain this discrete lattice information while connecting microscopic interactions to the energetics of finite contacts. Here, we develop a unified energy-density framework for rigid van der Waals interfaces by expressing registry-dependent pair potentials and atomic densities in reciprocal space. The resulting formulation accommodates different lattice bases and atomic species, linking single-atom and molecular adsorption to infinite bilayers and finite crystalline contacts. Explicit expressions for circular and regular polygonal flakes separate the area contribution from boundary-dependent terms and connect microscopic corrugation coefficients to energy barriers, rotational torques, and interlayer shear stiffnesses. The boundary analysis recovers the quarter-power area scaling of the barrier envelope for circular flakes and distinguishes bounded oscillations from square-root area scaling for polygonal contacts according to edge orientation. A dimensionless criterion characterizes the polygon-to-circle crossover in terms of moir\'e wavelength, flake size, and side number. Direct-summation benchmarks support the finite-domain expressions, while calculations for two-dimensional ice on graphene demonstrate the corresponding boundary-scaling trends in a molecular lattice. Applications to interlayer shear and graphite compression connect the same microscopic interaction description to tangential and normal mechanical responses. The framework establishes an analytical connection between microscopic registry, moir\'e periodicity, and finite-domain geometry, providing a basis for understanding and tailoring the energetics and mechanics of van der Waals contacts.

papers.title: Atomistic insight into defect-mediated boron redistribution and high-temperature strengthening in TiAl alloys
papers.abstract: Boron (B) microalloying can effectively refine microstructures of as-cast TiAl alloys and regulate their mechanical properties. Yet, how dilute B exists in TiAl and interacts with defects and how these interactions govern high-temperature deformation remain elusive. Here, we systematically elucidate defect-mediated B redistribution in TiAl alloys and its consequences for their deformation using hybrid grand-canonical Monte Carlo/molecular dynamics simulations augmented with a newly developed high-fidelity machine-learning potential. As a typical product of B microalloying, borides are markedly stiffer than the TiAl matrix and act as brittle reinforcing phases, while borides/matrix interfacial adhesion depends on surface termination and stacking sequence. In the bulk, interstitial B tends to be trapped at Ti-rich octahedral sites by high migration barriers but can kinetically evolve into substitutional dopants upon approaching Al vacancies. Increased tensile stress and vacancy concentration further promote B enrichment in the bulk. B is enriched at semi-coherent $\gamma/\alpha_2$ boundaries and preferentially partitions into the $\alpha_2$ phase. In polycrystalline TiAl, B accumulates primarily in disordered regions, raising the average flow stress by 9.4% at 1 at.% B and 900 K. This strengthening is accompanied by reduced shear strain accumulation. Simulated microstructural evolution and stacking-fault energetics indicate that B impedes dislocation glide via local pinning and suppresses deformation twinning, thereby increasing resistance to plastic deformation. By linking solute redistribution to defect interactions and deformation, these findings establish an atomistic framework for understanding and designing high-performance alloys based on interstitial solutes.

papers.title: High-Throughput Screening of Phononic Bandgap in Experimentally Realized Materials
papers.abstract: Materials with a phonon band gap offer a unique mechanism to restrict phonon scattering, making them promising candidates for developing functional materials for targeted thermal applications. Unlocking this mechanism across broad material classes requires systematic exploration, but first-principles methods and experiments are too expensive. Here, we used the universal machine-learning interatomic potential to quantify phonons and thermodynamic properties. We validated the accuracy of machine-learning-calculated results by comparing them with density-functional theory. We screened 154,879 materials and performed phonon calculations for 42,347 thermodynamically stable and experimentally observed compounds. We then performed phonon band gap analysis for dynamically stable materials and identified 11,176 materials with a phononic gap, including 10,960 materials with optical-optical gaps and 270 with acoustic-optical gaps. We also analyzed the lattice thermal conductivity of materials with phonon band gaps to identify candidates with acoustic-optical gaps and low thermal conductivity. Finally, by solving the linearized phonon Boltzmann equation from first principles, we demonstrate low room-temperature lattice thermal conductivities in three Li-metal binaries.

papers.title: Nonempirical Determination of the Optimal TAO-DFT Fictitious Temperature for Molecular Systems in the Lowest Singlet State
papers.abstract: Thermally-assisted-occupation density functional theory (TAO-DFT) [J.-D. Chai, J. Chem. Phys., 2012, ${\bf 136}$, 154104] has been developed to investigate the ground-state properties of large electronic systems exhibiting varying multi-reference (MR) character. As a central parameter in TAO-DFT, the fictitious temperature $\theta$ is closely linked to the degree of static correlation in an electronic system. While the conventional system-independent $\theta$-scheme is computationally efficient and broadly applicable, a fixed, preassigned $\theta$ can be overly large for single-reference (SR) systems yet too small for strongly MR systems. To overcome this limitation, we propose a nonempirical scheme based on spin-symmetry restoration to determine the optimal system-dependent fictitious temperature $\theta^{*}$ for molecular systems in their lowest singlet states. Across benchmark tests encompassing both MR systems (the bond dissociation of H$_{2}$, N$_{2}$, Li$_{2}$, and LiH, as well as the torsional rotation of twisted ethylene) and pure SR systems (the dissociation of He$_{2}$ and Ne$_{2}$), our nonempirical approach demonstrates superior overall accuracy compared with the conventional fixed-$\theta$ scheme. Furthermore, relative to standard Kohn-Sham density functional theory (TAO-DFT with $\theta = 0$), TAO-DFT employing $\theta^{*}$ yields substantial improvements for MR systems while preserving comparable accuracy in SR systems.

papers.title: High-Accuracy Neural-Network Quantum States via Randomized Real-Time Dynamics
papers.abstract: Neural-network quantum states (NQSs) exhibit a disparity in converging to the ground state during energy minimization: while the energy converges quadratically with the error in the variational wave function, other observables converge only linearly, which limits the accuracy of physical predictions. Here we show how to close this gap by introducing a new algorithm that improves the accuracy of NQSs. Our method, termed dynamical averaging, estimates expectation values by averaging over a state (or observable) evolved in real-time. Using insights from quantum information, we prove an up-to-quadratic suppression of error in arbitrary ground state observables, thus matching the fast convergence of the energy. Importantly, this improved accuracy requires neither further energy minimization nor increased model complexity, but rather exploits the effect of randomization on quantum states. We demonstrate dynamical averaging on non-integrable spin models, where it accelerates convergence and substantially reduces errors in observables.

papers.title: Growing Knot Embeddings into Spherical Graphs
papers.abstract: Knotted structures occur throughout soft matter and biology, where topological constraints can shape relaxation and spatial organization. Here, we introduce a computational construction that maps a specific 3D knot embedding to a graph embedded on the sphere through growth and interfacial-energy relaxation. For standard 3D embeddings of prime knots with at most seven crossings, we obtain a family of growth-based graphs that generally differ from the corresponding Tait graphs. We further identify an empirical growth-graph reconstruction rule based on polygonal regions with alternating crossing structure in a knot diagram. Non-minimal diagrams demonstrate that these graphs are not knot invariants, while selected connected sums suggest that graph features associated with their prime factors can remain recognizable. Determining how these graphs transform under isotopy may reveal invariant features, which we leave for future study.

papers.title: Geometry-conditioned differentiable surrogate with adjoint Monte Carlo sampling for scintillator detector co-design
papers.abstract: Optimizing light-guide geometries for scintillator-based imaging detectors requires repeated photon-transport evaluations, making direct Monte Carlo simulation computationally costly. Differentiable surrogates can accelerate these evaluations and support detector readout co-design aimed at improving information extraction from particle interactions. In this work we describe a surrogate model for photon transport. We develop it starting from a modular, event-driven Monte Carlo model for the generation and transport of scintillation photons, and a reciprocal Monte Carlo construction (an adjoint model) of a spatially and temporally resolved optical response field. The latter evaluates the collectible light output and its temporal structure from a scintillator volume by launching weighted photon trajectories from the light-guide readout face. We apply this approach to a scintillator cell with two mirrored, curved, single-clad light guides. We employ the adjoint model to train a geometry-conditioned neural surrogate that predicts collection probabilities and conditional transport-time distributions across a constrained guide-design family. The surrogate is natively differentiable, lending itself to be an element of a differentiable pipeline for gradient-based optimization. A forward-reciprocal benchmark and validation on held-out geometries establish the accuracy of the trained model and identify its limitations. The developed tools provide a foundation for rapid optical-response studies and detector readout co-design.

papers.title: Lincege.jl: LINked Cluster Expansions on a GEneral GEometry
papers.abstract: The numerical linked-cluster expansion (NLCE) is a powerful tool for studying properties of quantum lattice models directly in the thermodynamic limit. Here, we introduce Lincege.jl, a versatile, efficient, and easy-to-use package for generating the clusters needed to perform the NLCE on a general finite or infinite lattice. Lincege.jl takes as input only the Bravais lattice vectors, the basis information, and the expansion unit and uses a depth-first search to efficiently generate clusters, their lattice constants, and the sub-cluster information. It outputs final coefficients of the series, expressed in terms of the extensive properties of the clusters, in different orders. The package also contains tools for visualizing the lattice and the generated clusters as well as a classical Ising model solver that can be used as a template for interfacing Lincege.jl with solvers of other lattice models. This package can be installed using the Julia package manager and utilized with example scripts from our GitHub repository at https://github.com/rightleftspin/Lincege.jl. The online documentation, including examples, can be found at https://rightleftspin.github.io/Lincege.jl/stable/.

papers.title: Data handling, production, and simulation in the Muon g-2 Experiment at Fermilab
papers.abstract: This paper details the computing strategies of the Muon g-2 Experiment at Fermilab, which measured the muon's anomalous magnetic moment with a precision of 127 ppb by processing over 10 petabytes of detector and simulation data. This paper discusses the computational and operational challenges of data production, data handling, and data analysis of such large datasets. These challenges were overcome by using Fermilab-developed software infrastructure and production tools, making efficient use of resources, and improving the collaboration-developed reconstruction workflow. By overcoming these challenges, the experiment improved the data throughput capacity and reduced the analysis turnaround time by an order of magnitude over the course of its lifetime.

papers.title: Coarse-Grained Description of Stochastic Neutron Transport in Highly Heterogeneous Reactor Media via Non-Local Feller Boundary Functionals
papers.abstract: This paper presents a novel hierarchical coarse-graining framework to model non-Markovian neutron transport within the ultra-heterogeneous, multi-phase subcooled nucleate boiling layer of a nuclear reactor core. By applying Feller's subordination theory to continuous-time random walks, microscopic fluid fluctuations and vapor bubble dynamics are rigorously integrated into macroscopic transport operators through the apparatus of Complete Bernstein Functions (CBF). A modified non-local Fick's law is derived using a $P_1$-Legendre polynomial expansion, mapping the fractal porosity and structural phase boundaries into a stochastically renormalized effective diffusion coefficient. The thermodynamic consistency of the model is grounded within Chentsov's statistical manifolds, demonstrating that granular Poisson-like shot noise yields a geometric-exponential family of distributions characterized by a constant negative information curvature. To evaluate operational safety margins under transient conditions, a generalized Lyapunov functional with a quadratic memory kernel is constructed, and a complex decomposition of the transfer function $H(\omega)$ is performed. The resulting analytical limits are parameterized for a WWER-1000 core layout and translated into an engineering computational sequence suitable for implementation in Mathcad Prime 8 to diagnose the onset of Hopf bifurcations and spatial power oscillations.

papers.title: LayerCake v1.0: a framework for low- to intermediate-order automated models development
papers.abstract: A new model development framework called LayerCake is presented. It is written in the Python language and relies on the Sympy symbolic computation package to compute the Galerkin projection of two-dimensional spatially extended geophysical models. These projections provide their time evolution operator in the spectral space on a restricted set of modes. The resulting tendencies of the models can be evaluated either numerically (for time integration) or symbolically (for parameters sensitivity analysis and bifurcation analysis). We provide several simple examples of geophysical models to showcase the capabilities of the framework, and we hint at how more complex systems can be designed.
